surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A small invitation Two puzzle pieces to try together When fitting puzzle pieces becomes interesting, Davies suggests showing a turn or offering two jigsaw pieces that fit together. More pieces can come later. Start by noticing Your child is trying to fit pieces together and a knob puzzle may no longer offer enough challenge. Age, interest & context In the book: The chapter moves from puzzles from about 18 months to jigsaws as a next step, without giving a separate jigsaw starting age. Interest in fitting shapes together; choose difficulty by the number of pieces and offer two fitting pieces or a demonstration. A jigsaw adds a different question from a knob puzzle: how do the pieces join? Davies describes children trying the shapes spatially, rather than starting with corners and edges as adults often do. You can show how two pieces fit, then leave them for your child to explore. Help with a turn if needed, or return to an easier puzzle. Supervise small parts. She places this interest around 2½ in the chapter; small objects need adult supervision. In the everyday Your child wants to feel around an object without looking at it. Age, interest & context In the book: Around 2.5 years in the chapter and illustrated example; around 2+ years in the appendix. Interest in identifying an object by touch; distinct shapes are easier to distinguish. This broad band includes the earlier and later parts of the third year; follow the stated interest and help, not the birthday alone. Choose objects with clearly different shapes, such as a spoon and a key, in a bag that is hard to peek into. The child can feel for an object you name or discover what is inside by touch. Her examples use objects on a theme or matching pairs; a mixture of unrelated objects is harder. The appendix suggests five to eight objects and labels the activity around 2 years and older. These are differing starting descriptions, not a test to complete at either age. Age, interest & context In the book: Around 2 years; the child needs some spoken language. Some spoken language, with a shared real experience to talk about naturally. While preparing food or doing the laundry, you might remember planting something together and wonder where you put it or what you used. Davies describes this as a natural conversation, rather than a round of questions to answer correctly. Listen without finishing the sentence for them. If their meaning is unclear, invite them to show you. Naming objects for a child is different from testing whether they know the names; the book reserves the formal naming test for children over 3. topicRows.html:
A perspective

How Davies introduces scissors

Davies describes supervised scissors practice while seated at a table: learning to hold the handles, then snipping a narrow strip. Her chapter begins around 18 months; her illustrated example and appendix say around 2 years.

↗

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective How Davies introduces scissors Davies describes supervised scissors practice while seated at a table: learning to hold the handles, then snipping a narrow strip. Her chapter begins around 18 months; her illustrated example and appendix say around 2 years. In the everyday Your child is interested in opening and closing the scissors with your supervision. Age, interest & context In the book: Around 18 months in chapter prose; around 2 years in the illustrated example; around 2+ years in the appendix. Seated supervised handling, beginning with opening and closing; the adult holds the card at first. The book gives different ages for these examples; the later variants are context, not expectations for this band. She specifies real scissors with rounded ends that cut well. At first a child may use two hands to open and close them. When introducing cutting, the adult holds a thin strip of sturdy card for the child to snip; holding both scissors and paper comes later as hand strength develops. The cut pieces can go into a bowl and then a little envelope closed with a sticker. Repeating the opening-and-closing movement can be the whole exploration for now. Supervision remains part of this activity at either age. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective A first stitch through a card Davies describes supervised sewing with a blunt needle and a card with prepared holes. Her chapter places simple sewing around 2½ years; the illustrated example and appendix begin from 2. In the everyday Your child is interested in guiding something through a hole and pulling it from the other side. Age, interest & context In the book: Around 2.5 years in chapter prose; from 2 years in the illustrated example and 2+ years in the appendix. Interest in the push, turn, and pull movement, with an adult showing and supervising. This broad band includes the earlier and later parts of the third year; follow the stated interest and help, not the birthday alone. Her first card is a small square with holes along a diagonal. The illustrated example uses a blunt darning needle and thread doubled and knotted at the end. Show the needle going into a hole, turn the card over, and pull it through; then try the next hole. A child may want to repeat just that movement, with help as needed. The book includes scissors in the sewing kit and requires supervision for small parts and sharp tools. Later shapes and elaborate sewing need not be part of this first exploration. Turning the matching nuts adds another movement, with adult supervision for small parts. In the everyday Your child wants to compare sizes, fit objects, or turn a nut while holding a bolt. Age, interest & context In the book: From around 2 years in the illustrated example; 2+ years in the appendix. Start by placing bolts in matching holes; turning nuts is a later part of this same material. Her example uses a wooden board with differently sized holes and a container of matching nuts and bolts. The child can begin by finding which bolt fits which hole. As the turning becomes interesting, one hand can hold the bolt while the other turns the nut. Organizing the pieces by size is another possibility; matching every piece is not required. Your child can join one part before taking on a longer sequence. In the everyday Your child is interested in washing, squeezing a sponge, or using a cloth during cleanup. Age, interest & context In the book: Around 2+ years in the appendix; the chapter discusses shared dishwashing without a separate starting age. Interest in part of the work; adult supervision and more help for a shorter sequence. Her washing example uses two tubs on a table, a small-handled brush or sponge, a transparent plastic jug, and a travel-sized bottle holding only a little dishwashing liquid. An apron, drying mitt, and hand cloth are nearby. For drying, she lays a cloth on the table, puts the bowl or glass on it, folds the cloth into it, presses, and unfolds. Show a slow movement and help with carrying; her general guidance uses two hands for a glass. Keep the work small enough to enjoy together. It may take longer or end after one part; the aim here is participation, not a finished pile of dishes. Your child may want to repeat just the spraying or wiping while you help with the rest. Start by noticing Your child wants to copy a spraying or wiping movement. Age, interest & context In the book: The home chart includes cleaning windows at 18 months to 3 years; the detailed appendix example says around 2+ years. Interest in spraying or wiping, with adult help and a manageable amount of water. The book gives different ages for these examples; the later variants are context, not expectations for this band. Davies groups the window tools together so they are ready for the job. Her detailed example uses a spray bottle with a cup of water, a small squeegee, and a chamois or cloth; adding vinegar is optional in the book. Show a slow movement and let your child try the part that interests them. Put out only as much as you want to clean up, keep a cloth ready, and stop before the shared work becomes overwhelming. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas An everyday situation A last turn before a toy goes When you are passing an outgrown toy to another child or family, Davies suggests helping your toddler understand where it is going and offering one last turn. In the everyday An outgrown toy is leaving the home, and your child still wants a turn with it. Age, interest & context In the book: Toddler-wide discussion; no numerical age is given. A real decision to pass an outgrown item on; the child may need a final turn and a visible explanation. She separates storing a toy for later rotation from letting an outgrown one leave the home. For something being passed on, the child can have a final play, put it in the box when finished, and help carry the box out. If the box cannot leave straight away, she puts it out of view so the child does not have to go through the parting again. This is a way to involve them in a real change, not a demand that they stop caring about the toy. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Moving along at their own pace Davies describes a low trike or balance bike moved along with the feet, with a pedal tricycle as a separate, later possibility. Interest and what the child can manage guide the choice. In the everyday Your child is interested in riding and a different way of moving may be appealing. Age, interest & context In the book: Appendix: foot-propelled riding at 14–16 months, pedal tricycles from 2½ years. Balance-bike photograph: from around 2 years, once tall enough. Interest and manageable movement; the photographed balance bike also requires the child to be tall enough. The book does not give a separate pedal-readiness test. The appendix’s 14–16 month foot-propelled examples fall within this band. The pictured balance bike and pedal tricycle have later labels; neither is expected here. Her appendix groups foot-propelled riding at 14–16 months. The photographed balance-bike example has a different label: from around 2 years, once the child is tall enough. Those are separate presentations, not a deadline to combine. In the balance-bike example, the child pushes with their feet and gradually explores coasting at their own pace. Davies describes a later move to a regular bike as something that often happens, not a promised result. The appendix introduces pedal tricycles from 2½ years. Pedaling is a different movement from pushing along with the feet; an age label does not replace watching what the child can manage. Riding is one of many movement possibilities alongside running, dancing and ball play. The examples are not a collection every family needs to buy. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Pressing, sticking, rolling Davies describes glue, clay, and play dough as chances to explore how materials change. These are shared, supervised explorations, with no model to copy. In the everyday Notice an interest in pressing shapes down or changing a material with the hands. Age, interest & context In the book: Gluing from around 18 months in the chapter; clay is around 16 to 18+ months in the appendix. Interest in pressing, applying glue, rolling, or manipulating material; supervise small parts and sharp tools. Her gluing example uses paper shapes with a small pot of glue and brush, or a glue stick. The movement is to apply glue, turn the shape, and press it onto paper; the appendix uses a few large shapes. Interest in a real part of shopping, such as a picture list or passing an item; adult help and time remain available. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 48, 51. Davies includes shopping among ordinary opportunities to contribute. A picture list can let a child look for what comes next with you, and unpacking can continue the shared job at home. The Baby authors suggest choosing a few useful sources when parenting information becomes overwhelming. Both books pair learning with observing your own child and seeking support for questions about their development.

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective When parenting advice feels like too much The Baby authors suggest choosing a few useful sources when parenting information becomes overwhelming. Both books pair learning with observing your own child and seeking support for questions about their development. In the everyday When another book, course, or opinion leaves you with more to keep up with. Learning can begin with a question about the child in front of you. The Baby authors include observation alongside reading and other resources, and explicitly say that it is possible to limit how much information you take in. Davies encourages learning about a child’s differences and getting the support they need. Courses, podcasts, and books are possibilities in her account; her adult-preparation chapter offers practices that may fit some families and not others. Neither list has to become your reading assignment. The books also make room for learning about things you enjoy beyond parenting. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective A moment with your full attention Both books value attention during ordinary time together. Davies acknowledges competing commitments and offers ways to turn toward a child without expecting an adult to attend to everything at once. In the everyday When you are together but your attention keeps moving elsewhere. The Baby authors suggest using care as time to connect, and sometimes simply holding and enjoying a baby without another purpose. These can be moments within the day you already have. When a child wants to talk, Davies describes either pausing to listen or telling them when she can listen after finishing her task. She also sometimes writes down a distracting thought for later or puts her phone away so that she is less tempted to check it. The Baby authors make a similar distinction about photographs: pictures can hold memories, and the adult can be in some of them, but every moment need not be recorded. These are possibilities for attention and enjoyment, not a demand to document family life. topicRows.text: A perspective Honest words can still be kind Both books invite adults to model truthfulness with sensitivity. Davies offers everyday examples of stating a limit or making a truthful observation without an invented excuse. ↗
topicRows.html:
A perspective

Honest words can still be kind

Both books invite adults to model truthfulness with sensitivity. Davies offers everyday examples of stating a limit or making a truthful observation without an invented excuse.

↗

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Honest words can still be kind Both books invite adults to model truthfulness with sensitivity. Davies offers everyday examples of stating a limit or making a truthful observation without an invented excuse. In the everyday When you are tempted to give a convenient excuse rather than say what you mean. For a call she does not want to take, Davies suggests saying that she is tired and asking to speak later. Her example makes the adult’s limit clear without pretending to be occupied with something else. When asked about a haircut she does not like, she offers a truthful observation about the person’s pleasure in it. The point is to look for words that are both accurate and considerate. The Baby authors likewise include sensitive truthfulness in their adaptation of don Miguel Ruiz’s Four Agreements. Davies acknowledges that finding kind, honest words takes practice. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Notice your own limit before it builds Davies suggests noticing an approaching limit and expressing it kindly before irritation builds. The Baby authors also invite reflection on the adult’s own needs, without turning it into a judgment of their parenting. In the everyday When a familiar situation leaves you increasingly tired, frustrated, or stretched. Notice what you are feeling and what you need, as well as what your child needs. Davies describes adult limits as part of balancing the people in a family, and says that following the child leaves room for the adult too. If you can only make sense of a difficult response later, both books make room for that. The Baby authors suggest reflecting on what drove a reaction and what might have helped; Davies includes thinking or writing later, with compassion. Davies’s appendix offers feelings and needs vocabulary contributed by Yoram Mosenzon. For example, noticing tiredness and a need for rest can give you more to work with than blaming another person. The table is an aid to reflection, not a test of what you ought to feel. Reflection sits alongside receiving care: both books include asking others for help, and they direct readers toward a doctor for depression. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Give time with something you enjoy A song, a shared book, or a story from your own life can be a gift of time. Both books value what caregivers enjoy sharing; Davies also recognizes that giving a present can express love. In the everyday When a relative or caregiver wants a way to share something with your child. The Baby authors describe grandparents and caregivers bringing music, stories, history, and culture into family life. Their letter to visitors invites adults to share their own interests. Davies suggests choosing an interest that can be shared with the child, or spending time together outdoors. A book enjoyed together is another of her examples. Her gift suggestions emphasize being together and can also include giving a parent some respite. Paid outings are among her examples, but a purchased experience is not required to share a song or story. topicRows.text: A perspective Get to know each twin The Baby authors suggest using each child’s name and noticing their needs individually. Being the same age does not require treating the children as a single unit. ↗
topicRows.html:
A perspective

Get to know each twin

The Baby authors suggest using each child’s name and noticing their needs individually. Being the same age does not require treating the children as a single unit.

↗

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Get to know each twin The Baby authors suggest using each child’s name and noticing their needs individually. Being the same age does not require treating the children as a single unit. In the everyday For families with twins, while getting to know what is particular to each child. Look at what each child is interested in and what help each needs. The authors suggest calling them by their names, rather than referring to them only as “the twins.” They also describe involving both children in daily life as their skills grow. Their examples invite participation and taking turns; they do not require buying two of every toy. The chapter recognizes the practical work of caring for two children of the same age. For example, it explicitly says that simultaneous breastfeeding may be possible and is also okay if it is not manageable. This is an acknowledgment of family capacity, not a feeding instruction. Back to the books The Montessori Baby Twins Individual names and needs, gradual participation, toy turns and adult capacity PDF pp. 228–229 Paraphrased for this companion. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective A wider circle of familiar people Both books describe family life among relatives, friends, caregivers, and people in the neighborhood. The Baby authors recognize that parenting can feel isolated and invite families to build connections from the people available to them. In the everyday When you want company or familiar connections beyond the people at home. This circle can include friends with children and friends with whom you talk about other interests. The Baby authors also name neighbors and people in local shops whose faces become familiar through everyday life. For relatives who live far away, they suggest sharing books, songs, or music over a video call, with in-person visits when possible. It is one way to stay connected across distance. Davies includes relatives and people who are not related to you within the family’s wider community. These are possibilities for connection, not a list of relationships every family must maintain. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas An everyday situation When your child asks for the other parent Davies describes acknowledging a toddler’s wish for a different parent while the available parent offers care. She also suggests considering recent family changes, without treating one explanation as true for every child. In the everyday When your toddler wants one parent for dressing, bathing, reading, or another familiar part of the day. Age, interest & context In the book: Davies describes toddlers as around 1 to 3 years. A toddler repeatedly asks for one parent to give care. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. The parent who is present can put the wish into words and explain that they are helping this time. Davies pairs this clarity with gentleness and understanding. Travel, a new baby, or moving home are among the changes she suggests considering. A toddler may need extra understanding and closeness; their request does not by itself establish why they feel this way. Davies acknowledges that repeated preference can feel upsetting or alienating for the other parent. She introduces these ideas as possibilities, with no single approach that fits every family. topicRows.text: A small invitation Take turns hearing each other out For an everyday disagreement with a trusted caregiver who is willing to talk, Davies offers a listening exercise: hear their concern, reflect back what you understood, invite correction, then switch roles. ↗
topicRows.html:
A small invitation

Take turns hearing each other out

For an everyday disagreement with a trusted caregiver who is willing to talk, Davies offers a listening exercise: hear their concern, reflect back what you understood, invite correction, then switch roles.

↗

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A small invitation Take turns hearing each other out For an everyday disagreement with a trusted caregiver who is willing to talk, Davies offers a listening exercise: hear their concern, reflect back what you understood, invite correction, then switch roles. Start by noticing When you both want to understand a disagreement but keep talking past each other. Davies adapts an exercise from Scilla Elworthy’s 2017 Montessori Congress address. She proposes asking whether the other person has twenty minutes: five for them to speak, five for you to reflect what you heard, then the same two turns with the roles reversed. Reflect both the words and the feelings you think you heard. The speaker can correct a misunderstanding. Naming another person’s feelings is an invitation to check your understanding, not deciding for them. Davies pairs the exercise with observations, statements about your own feelings and needs, and requests that leave room for other solutions. The Baby authors similarly suggest agreeing on a time to talk; if tiredness or strong feelings make that difficult, they describe proposing a specific later time and returning to it. Back to the books The Montessori Toddler When there is conflict in the family Elworthy attribution, voluntary twenty-minute exercise, reversal and correction, requests PDF pp. 209–210 The Montessori Baby Getting on the same page / Communicate in a way that we will (more likely) be heard Agreeing a time, mutual perspectives and rescheduling when not ready PDF pp. 249–251 Paraphrased for this companion. Illustrations are original and illustrative. You don’t need a different home. Start with what you have. She proposes asking whether the other person has twenty minutes: five for them to speak, five for you to reflect what you heard, then the same two turns with the roles reversed. Age, interest & context In the book: Before 2.5 years mainly parallel play; around 2.5 years possible shared play, sometimes earlier with siblings or regular peer contact. Observe whether both children welcome watching or joining, and when one wants to play alone. The book describes a possible change around 2½, not an expectation throughout this age band. Before about 2½, Davies describes toddlers as mainly playing alongside each other. She notes that children with siblings or regular peer company may share earlier. These are broad observations, rather than a timetable for a particular child. Even when children want to play together, they may need help finding words or noticing that the other child has finished sharing the moment. Davies describes acknowledging that one child wants to play alone and returning for a turn later. Her turn-taking approach supports the child already using an activity and the child waiting. The adult still steps in to stop pushing or grabbing. In a shared public place, she allows a shorter ending so someone else can have a turn. Her prose says around 3, while the recap says over 3; this is not a setup instruction for every child in the 2–3-year band. Age, interest & context In the book: Older toddler around 3 years old in PDF136; child over 3 years old in PDF138. The source specifies voluntary use, not a readiness test; these differing ages do not establish suitability below 3. Included as book context near the third birthday, with no under-three calm-space procedure. The idea is attributed to Jane Nelsen. In Davies’s description, a child chooses whether to use the space and how long to stay. It is never a threat or an imposed time-out, and an adult can offer to go along. The prose and recap also describe suggesting more time there if a child remains upset. That sits within the wider guidance to stay available, offer rather than insist on touch, and act immediately to stop harm. It does not make comfort conditional on being calm. For the toddler years, Davies’s recurring sequence is support through the feeling, reconnection after calm, and help making amends when needed. The differing calm-place ages should not become a reason to send a younger child away. The authors ask families to consider a setting as it is today. In the everyday When you need or want someone else to care for your baby. Age, interest & context A perspective from The Montessori Baby on choosing care; its discussion includes the first three years. The authors describe patient, responsive caregivers who enjoy babies, attend to their signals, and support parents. Familiar, consistent caregivers matter in their account. They acknowledge that one-to-one care or a Montessori program may be unavailable or outside a family’s budget. A warm setting without a Montessori label may suit a family better than one that applies the principles more strictly. Their question is whether the care feels acceptable as it currently works, without relying on the provider changing later. They offer possible alternatives when it does not fit, while recognizing that families have different options. What’s underneath The relationship and the family’s real options matter when choosing care. The authors favor direct, sensory exploration over passive screen entertainment. In the everyday When you are considering the place of screens in family life. Age, interest & context In the book: The authors recommend no screens before two and little or none after two. This describes the Baby book’s perspective on family screen use. Age, interest & context An adult perspective on the words and opportunities offered during the early years. Notice whether a quality or activity is being offered only to one gender. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective When preschool is coming up For families preparing for preschool or school, Davies describes familiar everyday participation, getting to know another caregiver, and adult help with social moments. These can be part of preparing for the change. In the everyday When your family has an upcoming preschool or school start. Age, interest & context For an actual upcoming start; the book gives no starting age here. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Her everyday examples include a jacket, shoes, and a tissue. An adult can support the part the child is trying; these examples do not need to become a list of skills to pass before school. If another caregiver is new, Davies suggests first spending time together reading or playing. Once the child is comfortable with that person, she describes short separations that can gradually become longer. She emphasizes telling the child when you leave, even when goodbye brings sadness. In her account of working with other caregivers, she also recalls using a brief, warm goodbye and offering a hug at reunion if her child wanted one. At the playground, she describes translating a child’s meaning, helping them stand up for themselves when needed, and modeling care for other people. Preparing can include this adult support. Back to the books The Montessori Toddler Getting ready for preschool/school Everyday participation, a familiar caregiver and social support PDF p. 213 The Montessori Toddler What makes an activity Montessori?; How to show the child an activity Partial participation and help when frustrated PDF pp. 34–35 The Montessori Toddler The key to working together as a family / Working with others Davies’s short goodbye, letting the child know about leaving, and a wanted hug at reunion PDF p. 206 Paraphrased for this companion. Illustrations are original and illustrative. You don’t need a different home. Start with what you have. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Enjoy a new skill without a demonstration Both books suggest noticing what a child chooses to do instead of asking them to perform a new skill on cue. Naming what interests them and sharing curiosity can keep the exchange going. In the everyday When you want to show someone what your child has been trying. Age, interest & context Guidance for the adult’s response to a child’s discoveries; no skill demonstration is expected. Davies recalls asking her son to demonstrate things for relatives, then deciding to stop these tests and watch for what he showed in his own time. Her story offers a way to enjoy a child’s discoveries without needing a performance. In The Montessori Toddler, she distinguishes a test with one expected answer from a question that invites curiosity. She makes an exception when she is certain the child knows an answer and is excited to share it, which she describes as usually starting around three. The child’s interest matters in that example. Back to the books The Montessori Baby Being their guide / Removing obstacles Davies’s recollection of asking her son to demonstrate skills PDF pp. 111–113 The Montessori Toddler General principles / Avoid quizzing the child Observation and curiosity in place of tests, with the eager-child exception around three PDF pp. 36–39 Paraphrased for this companion. Illustrations are original and illustrative. You don’t need a different home. Start with what you have.
